chapter.title: A First Model
chapter.para: In this chapter we develop a program that can tell two kinds of points apart. We begin with a single neuron and then build, from layers of neurons, a small network that finds its own weights.

section.title: Two Kinds of Points
section.para: Let there be a plane with the coordinates x and y, each from -6 to +6. Into this plane we put points of two kinds: orange and blue. In the programs the kind of a point is represented by a number: 1 for orange and -1 for blue.

A model is a function that computes, from the coordinates x and y of a place in this plane, a guess of the kind of a point at that place: a value between -1 and +1. At -1 the model is sure that a blue point lies there; at +1 it predicts an orange one with certainty. Values in between express uncertainty: the sign says which kind the model leans to, and the nearer the value is to 0, the less sure it is; at 0 it cannot decide.
We could write such a function any way we like, for example

mediaobject.alt: The plane coloured by f(x, y) = x / 6: blue on the left, orange on the right, pale in the middle.

section.para: It is +1 at the right edge, -1 at the left and 0 on the upright axis: on the right it guesses orange, on the left blue, and the nearer the middle, the less sure it is. Or

mediaobject.alt: The plane coloured by the cosine model: an orange disc in the middle, blue corners.

section.para: It is +1 at the centre, because cos⁡0=1, and -1 in the four corners, because there x2+y2=36+36=72 and cos⁡π=−1; on the circle of radius 6 around the centre it is 0. Whether such a function guesses well depends on the points: the first suits points that are orange on the right and blue on the left, the second an orange disc in a blue ring.

Machine learning, on the other hand, does not make the formula up. It fixes only its general form, a formula with numbers left open, the parameters. In the second example the 72 could be such an open number, f⁡(x,y)=cos⁡(π(x2+y2)/c), and c would decide how large the orange disc is. Which values the parameters get, a program finds out from examples, points whose kind is known. Finding them is what this book calls learning, and a function with its parameters found a trained model.

sidebar.para: Open the page with the second model and move c back and forth: the colouring follows the formula. A large c makes the orange disc large; a small one makes rings appear.

section.title: One Neuron
section.para: The simplest form of such a function is a neuron. It multiplies each of its inputs by a number of its own, its weight, adds them up and adds one more number, its bias:

Where z is positive the neuron guesses orange, where it is negative, blue. The points where z is exactly 0 form a straight line, so a neuron parts the plane by a line: the weights turn it, the bias moves it. Here is a neuron with weights we chose, 1 and 1 and a bias of 0, looking at six points:
section.screen: (2, 1.5) is 1: z = 3.5, the guess 1, right (1, 3) is 1: z = 4, the guess 1, right (0.5, -2.5) is 1: z = -2, the guess -1, wrong (-2, -1) is -1: z = -3, the guess -1, right (-1, -3) is -1: z = -4, the guess -1, right (-3, 1) is -1: z = -2, the guess -1, right
section.para: Five of the six are right. The point (0.5, -2.5) is orange but lies below the line x+y=0. Set w2 to 0 and run it again: the line becomes the upright axis, x=0, and all six are right. Turning the line by changing a weight until the guesses are right is exactly what learning will do, only by itself.

section.title: How Wrong
section.para: To change the weights by itself a program needs a number that says how wrong the neuron is, a number that gets smaller as the neuron gets better. Counting the wrong guesses does not serve: a small change of a weight usually changes no guess at all, so the count does not say which way to turn.
So the neuron's sum is first squashed into a number between -1 and 1 by a smooth function, here the hyperbolic tangent:

Now the neuron answers as the beginning of the chapter asked of a model: near +1 or -1 where it is sure, near 0 where it is not. Such a squashing function is the neuron's activation, and a its answer. Now the answer can be compared with the kind t the point really has:

This is the loss of one point: 0 where the answer is exactly the kind, larger the further it is from it, and every small change of a weight changes it a little. The loss of the model is the mean of the losses of all points.

section.title: Downhill
section.para: Think of the loss as a landscape. Each choice of the three numbers w1, w2 and b is a place in it, and the loss there is its height. Learning is walking downhill. Which way is down can be read off each weight separately: how much does the loss change when the weight changes a little? That is the weight's derivative, written ∂L/∂w1.
The loss does not depend on w1 directly. It depends on the answer a, the answer on the sum z, and the sum on w1. Each link of that chain has a slope that is easy to say:

listitem.para: the loss by the answer: a−t;
the answer by the sum, the slope of tanh: 1−a2;
the sum by the weight: x, the input the weight multiplies.

section.para: The chain rule says that the slope of the whole chain is the product of the slopes of its links:

For w2 the last factor is y, for the bias it is 1. Added up over all points and divided by their number, these derivatives are the gradient: the direction in which the loss rises fastest. One step of gradient descent moves every weight a little the other way,

mediaobject.alt: The loss over the two weights, dark in a valley to the right; the walk of gradient descent runs down into it.

section.para: where the small number η is the learning rate. The program below starts the neuron of the last section from weights that guess badly and takes a hundred such steps:
section.programlisting:
; One neuron learns: it starts from weights that guess badly, measures how ; wrong it is, and moves each weight a little the way that makes it less so. define Point(x: f64, y: f64, kind: f64)
; A number shown to three places. function shown(v: f64) returns f64 { (v * 1000.0).round_even() / 1000.0 }
var points Array[Point]() points.add(Point(2.0, 1.5, 1.0)) points.add(Point(1.0, 3.0, 1.0)) points.add(Point(0.5, 0.0 - 2.5, 1.0)) points.add(Point(0.0 - 2.0, 0.0 - 1.0, 0.0 - 1.0)) points.add(Point(0.0 - 1.0, 0.0 - 3.0, 0.0 - 1.0)) points.add(Point(0.0 - 3.0, 1.0, 0.0 - 1.0)) let n points.length as f64
var w1 0.0 - 0.5 var w2 0.5 var b 0.0 let rate 0.1 var step 0 while step <= 100 { ; how wrong it is, and which way each weight should go var loss 0.0 var right 0 var g1 0.0 var g2 0.0 var gb 0.0 for p in points { let a tanh(w1 * p.x + w2 * p.y + b) let e a - p.kind loss := loss + 0.5 * e * e if a * p.kind > 0.0 right := right + 1 let dz e * (1.0 - a * a) g1 := g1 + dz * p.x g2 := g2 + dz * p.y gb := gb + dz } if step % 10 = 0 print "step `step`: loss `shown(loss / n)`, `right` of 6 right" w1 := w1 - rate * g1 / n w2 := w2 - rate * g2 / n b := b - rate * gb / n step := step + 1 } print "w1 `shown(w1)`, w2 `shown(w2)`, b `shown(b)`"
section.screen: step 0: loss 0.941, 2 of 6 right step 10: loss 0.325, 5 of 6 right step 20: loss 0.112, 5 of 6 right step 30: loss 0.06, 6 of 6 right step 40: loss 0.043, 6 of 6 right step 50: loss 0.033, 6 of 6 right step 60: loss 0.027, 6 of 6 right step 70: loss 0.023, 6 of 6 right step 80: loss 0.02, 6 of 6 right step 90: loss 0.018, 6 of 6 right step 100: loss 0.016, 6 of 6 right w1 1.158, w2 0.022, b 0.3
section.para: The loss falls from step to step, and after thirty steps every point is right. The weights it found are close to the ones we found by hand: w2 is nearly 0, the line nearly the upright axis. The for over the points adds up the gradient; Scaly may run its rounds on several cores, and a sum of floating-point numbers still comes out the same, because it is folded in the order of the points.

sidebar.para: Open the field with a learning rate of 0.001. The colours come only slowly, and the loss curve on the right creeps down. Choose 0.1 under Learning rate: the same network is done in a moment. Too small a step costs time; too large a one can overshoot the valley and make the loss jump instead of fall.

section.title: Better Inputs
section.para: A neuron parts the plane by a line, and some points no line can part. Put a disc of orange points inside a ring of blue ones: every line has orange and blue on both sides. The program below tries it twice, first with x and y as the neuron's inputs, then with their squares:
section.screen: given x and y: step 0: loss 0.5, 0 of 16 right step 100: loss 0.5, 7 of 16 right step 200: loss 0.5, 7 of 16 right step 300: loss 0.5, 7 of 16 right step 400: loss 0.5, 7 of 16 right given x² and y²: step 0: loss 0.5, 0 of 16 right step 100: loss 0.015, 16 of 16 right step 200: loss 0.007, 16 of 16 right step 300: loss 0.004, 16 of 16 right step 400: loss 0.003, 16 of 16 right
section.para: Given x and y, the neuron stays at a loss of 0.5, no better than not guessing at all. Given x2 and y2, it learns every point. The neuron still draws a line, but a line in the inputs it is given: w1x2+w2y2+b=0 is, on the plane, a circle. Choosing what a model sees is called feature engineering, and good inputs can make a hard problem easy.

sidebar.para: Open the circle with x and y as inputs. The output stays a straight edge between two pale halves. Click on x2 and y2 in the network to give them to the neuron, and on x and y to take those away: the edge closes into a circle. Each small square shows what one input or neuron answers over the whole plane.

section.title: Hidden Layers
section.para: For a disc the right inputs are easy to guess. For most data they are not, and here comes the idea that makes neural networks strong: let neurons compute the inputs. A hidden layer is a row of neurons that each read x and y and each draw a line of their own. Their answers are the inputs of one more neuron, the output, which combines the lines into regions: orange inside these two, blue outside this one.

The data that shows it best is called XOR: orange where x and y have the same sign, blue where they do not, the four quarters of the plane alternating. No single line parts them, but two lines do, with something to combine them.

sidebar.para: Open XOR without a hidden layer: the network finds nothing. With one hidden layer of three neurons it learns the four quarters. Look at the three squares of the hidden layer: each is a straight edge, one line, and the output's square is their combination. The lines between the squares are the weights, orange for positive, blue for negative, the thicker the stronger.

section.para: The activation matters here. Without one, a neuron reading neurons would add up sums of sums, which is again only a sum, one line; it is the bend in each neuron's answer that lets the layers do more than one neuron could. The field offers four: tanh, ReLU (the sum itself where it is positive, 0 elsewhere), sigmoid (like tanh, but between 0 and 1) and none at all, which shows exactly that failure.

section.title: Backpropagation
section.para: How does a hidden neuron learn? Its weights are as far from the loss as can be, behind the output neuron. The chain rule still answers, with a chain one link longer, and the clever part is the order in which it is computed.

First everything is computed forward, as before: each hidden neuron's answer hj, then the output's sum and its answer a. Then backward. The output neuron's share of the error, the loss by its sum, is the familiar

and its weights' derivatives follow from it as for a single neuron: dhj for the weight vj that reads hidden neuron j. Hidden neuron j reaches the loss through that weight, so its answer's slope is dvj, and through its own tanh its share of the error becomes

From there its weights are once more a single neuron's: djx, djy and dj for its bias. The error is handed back through the network layer by layer, each layer's share computed from the share of the layer after it. That is backpropagation, and it is the whole secret of how networks of any depth learn. Here it is written out for XOR, with three hidden neurons:
section.screen: step 0: loss 0.52, 2 of 4 right step 50: loss 0.025, 4 of 4 right step 100: loss 0.006, 4 of 4 right step 150: loss 0.003, 4 of 4 right step 200: loss 0.002, 4 of 4 right step 250: loss 0.002, 4 of 4 right step 300: loss 0.001, 4 of 4 right
section.para: The hidden neurons start from different weights on purpose. Had they all started alike, they would answer alike, get the same gradient in every step and stay alike forever, three copies of one line. The field starts its weights at random for the same reason.

section.title: What It Has Not Seen
section.para: A model that knows its training points is not yet useful. The question is how well it guesses points it has never seen. That is why the field holds back half of its points as test points, drawn with a ring: the network never learns from them, and the loss over them, the test loss, says how well it generalizes.

When the data is noisy and the network large, the two losses part ways. The network learns the training points ever better, noise included, and draws borders around single stray points; the test loss stops falling and rises. That is overfitting. One cure is regularization: an extra loss for large weights, λw2 for each weight. Its derivative shrinks every weight a little in every step, and a network with smaller weights draws smoother borders.

sidebar.para: Open the spiral with 30 % noise and four hidden layers of eight. After some seconds the training loss is far below the test loss, and the plane shows islands around single points. Choose 0.01 under Regularization (L2) and Start again: the training loss stays higher, the test loss ends lower, the borders are smoother.

section.title: The Field's Program
section.para: The page runs one Scaly program, field.scaly, built for WebAssembly. It is this chapter's programs grown up: up to six hidden layers of up to eight neurons, seven inputs to choose from, four activations, regularization, and backpropagation as in the last section, only in loops over layers instead of written out. It keeps everything the page shows in one vector of numbers in its memory, which the page reads directly, without a copy; the picture of the network's answer over the plane is a for over its 6400 points, which Scaly spreads over the cores of the machine by itself. Its source is on GitHub.

Everything this chapter derived by hand, the chain rule through every link and the gradient of every weight, a program can derive too. That is the subject of the chapters ahead: first how Scaly holds many numbers at once, in tensors, then a tape that records the forward computation and plays it back to get every derivative.
